lessons.name: Workflow graphs and explicit state
lessons.role: Compare a fixed DAG/state machine, model-assisted node and model-directed tool choice on one task.
lessons.description: A workflow represents progress as state and permitted transitions. A node may compute a value, call a service, wait for input or select the next step. The important distinction is who chooses the transition and what evidence permits it. A fixed workflow follows authored control flow; a model-assisted workflow can use a prediction inside that flow; a model-directed system can propose its next operation from observations. None of these designs can turn a proposed tool call into an authorized effect by itself. The durable incident example compares a fixed workflow with an authored branching policy on the same environment and task. The latter can repair one malformed argument yet still choose the wrong manual fact. Its extra branches are visible source logic, not learned reasoning. Separating business state from the last message also makes the end condition testable: a worker can report completion while inventory or the work order is wrong.
mechanism: The incident identity, target asset and allowed effects define a task before any node executes.
A transition consumes the current state and a recorded event; each tool node passes through validation and authority.
A review state stores an exact proposed action and waits for a decision instead of treating the wait as failure.
The policy can stop, retry or choose a next tool, but the independent environment checker evaluates the completed business state.
lessons.learningObjective: Identify the owner of each transition and distinguish workflow completion from a satisfied external goal.
lessons.engineeringExample: For incident-017, both authored modes read FAN-7, obtain reference facts, reserve two FILTER-A units after review and create one linked work order. The normal run uses four calls. If the reference list begins with FAN-9, the fixed workflow selects the requested asset while the authored first-fact policy uses FAN-9. Both can reach their internal completed state. Only the FAN-7 environment satisfies the original goal. The comparison therefore measures the task after execution rather than rewarding a particular graph shape or the number of tool calls.
lessons.misconception: A graph containing an AI node is not automatically a model-directed agent.

options: The final environment matches the task and policy constraints

lessons.name: Events, queues and backpressure
lessons.role: Distinguish event occurrence, delivery, acknowledgement, deduplication, retries and admission.
lessons.description: An event describes something that occurred; a delivery is one attempt to bring that event to a consumer. Networks, acknowledgements and worker failures can cause repeated or delayed deliveries. A queue therefore holds deliveries, while the consumer may track stable business event identities. Admission moves a delivery into service; deduplication can remove a repeated identity without repeating its effects. Queue length alone says nothing about unique useful work. A retry policy must also distinguish a request that never started from one whose acknowledgement was lost. In the incident experience two simultaneous deliveries name the same incident. One worker handles it, then acknowledges the remaining duplicate without another reservation. This is a bounded single-consumer example; it does not implement a general distributed queue or prove exactly-once delivery.
mechanism: A stable event identity accompanies each delivery, separately from its arrival attempt.
The queue balance records arrivals, admissions into service and discarded duplicates at one declared boundary.
The consumer checks whether a delivery belongs to an already handled incident before beginning another workflow.
A durable effect still needs its own idempotency protection because a consumer may fail after service starts.
lessons.learningObjective: Reconcile arrivals, admissions and duplicate removals without confusing deliveries with distinct business tasks.
lessons.engineeringExample: Start with an empty queue and deliver incident-017 twice. The queue contains two deliveries. Admission removes one, leaving one waiting while the worker makes four normal tool calls. After completion, deduplication removes the second delivery, so the queue returns to zero. Exactly one reservation and one work order exist. Two arrivals minus one admission minus one duplicate removal equals zero queued deliveries; counting deliveries as two successful incidents would overstate useful work.
lessons.misconception: An acknowledgement retry does not necessarily represent a new task.

check.question: Two copies of the same incident arrive; one is admitted and one is deduplicated. How many distinct incidents were executed?
options: Two
One
Zero because a duplicate is an error
check.explanation: The stable incident identity is the same on both deliveries; only one workflow executes.

specs.label: Mechanism boundary
specs.value: Why does one event sometimes arrive twice?
specs.context: Counts share one queue boundary. Admissions and duplicate removals cannot exceed available queued deliveries. Business effects are counted separately.

lessons.name: Durable actions and the ambiguous timeout
lessons.shortName: Durable actions and the ambiguous timeout
lessons.role: Persist intent, execute with idempotency key, store receipt and recover without duplicate business effects.
lessons.description: A write can commit even when its response never reaches the caller. Retrying blindly then risks creating a second external effect; refusing every retry can leave a valid task unfinished. An idempotency key names one logical action, while a payload fingerprint records exactly which action that key refers to. The service stores an effect and its receipt together at its own boundary. A matching retry returns the original receipt; a changed payload under that key must not silently reuse or replace it. A workflow journal records intent before service and observations afterward. Those records can lag the external effect. The incident experience deliberately separates local journal and environment storage so an interrupted result write leaves a real reservation to recover. This is different from restoring neural weights or replaying lost arithmetic: an external reservation is already part of the world.
mechanism: Persist the approved action intent before starting the service that can mutate inventory.
The service validates the key and payload, commits one reservation and stores its original receipt.
If the response is lost, the caller records uncertainty rather than success or proof that nothing happened.
Receipt lookup or an identical idempotent retry recovers the outcome; conflicting arguments fail without another effect.
lessons.learningObjective: Explain the caller’s uncertainty and prove that recovery preserves one logical effect after a commit-before-response failure.
lessons.engineeringExample: FAN-7 begins with four FILTER-A units. The reservation for quantity two commits, leaving two units and receipt K. The response is lost. A repeat request carrying K and the same payload returns the original reservation: stock stays at two. A request carrying K but quantity one conflicts with its stored fingerprint and changes nothing. If result journaling itself fails, reload retains the committed environment and the pending intent; recovery reconciles that exact receipt before continuing to the work order.
lessons.misconception: A timeout is neither proof of nonexecution nor permission to issue a new logical action.

check.question: After the reservation committed but its reply was lost, what should the same-key retry do?
options: Reserve two more units
Return the original receipt without changing stock
Erase the first reservation
check.explanation: The service recognizes the same logical action and returns its already committed outcome.

specs.label: Mechanism boundary
specs.context: The key and payload are unchanged, receipt retention covers the retry, and the service atomically commits the effect and receipt. This is an effect guarantee under those assumptions, not an exactly-once network-delivery claim.

lessons.name: Tool schemas and semantic validation
lessons.role: Syntax, types, domain constraints, resource identity, output schema and result errors.
lessons.description: A tool contract defines a name, input fields and types, output structure and error behavior. It turns a proposed operation into something a runtime can inspect before execution. Schema validation is only the first boundary: valid identifiers may refer to the wrong resource, and a positive integer quantity may still conflict with available stock or supporting evidence. Semantic checks therefore compare the request with current domain state. Authority and human approval remain separate conditions, so adding an approval field to arbitrary JSON does not grant permission. The fixture reservation tool accepts a bounded integer quantity and rejects additional fields. Its actual implementation also checks the asset, stock and manual fact. Even a semantically valid action for FAN-9 can fail a task whose goal was FAN-7; no schema can replace that external goal check.
mechanism: The tool envelope selects a known operation and exactly the fields permitted by its input contract.
Type and range checks reject malformed values before authority checks or service.
Domain checks bind identifiers, evidence and current stock when the service executes.
The returned result has an explicit success or error meaning, while the final task checker remains independent.
lessons.learningObjective: Locate whether a failed call violates syntax, type, domain state, authority or the intended task.
lessons.engineeringExample: The authored malformed call sends quantity as the string "2". The numeric contract rejects it and no reservation service starts. The bounded policy then issues a new call with integer 2, which passes schema validation and still needs authority and exact review. In the wrong-entity case, integer 1 and a FAN-9 manual can be valid and internally consistent, yet they do not satisfy the FAN-7 task. Repairing syntax therefore changes only one layer of the evidence chain.
lessons.misconception: Well-formed JSON does not establish that an action is authorized or correct.

check.question: A valid reservation call targets FAN-9, but the task asks for FAN-7. Which check catches the remaining problem?
options: JSON parsing alone

check.explanation: A schema can validate the request shape while the requested entity remains wrong for this task.

lessons.name: User authority and service identity
lessons.role: User authorization, workload authentication, token audience, scope and resource policy are separate checks.
lessons.description: The person asking for work, the software making a request and the service receiving it are distinct principals. Authentication establishes an identity under a particular trust mechanism. Authorization evaluates whether that principal may perform a particular action on a particular resource. A service identity can be genuine while its request is outside the user’s permitted scope. Token audience and expiry also matter: possession of a token intended for one resource is not authority at every other service. Model output cannot create credentials or expand a capability. The incident fixture demonstrates a deliberately small role/capability gate: a read-only user can obtain asset and manual data but cannot reserve stock. It does not implement token issuance, OAuth, workload attestation or cryptographic signatures. Those mechanisms explain why a production boundary requires more than a prompt saying that an action is allowed.
mechanism: Identify the user, calling workload and receiving resource separately.
The receiver checks identity validity and the token’s intended audience under its actual authentication mechanism.
Scopes and resource policy constrain the requested action; user approval cannot silently broaden those scopes.
A denied write returns a reason and leaves the external environment unchanged.
lessons.learningObjective: Separate authentication, audience, scope, resource policy and action approval in a tool request.
lessons.engineeringExample: Consider a synthetic token with audience maintenance-api and scope asset:read. An authenticated read of FAN-7 can be allowed, but a reservation requires a write scope and the relevant resource policy. Sending that token to a payroll service should fail audience validation even if its signature is otherwise valid. In the local incident case the read-only role reaches a schema-valid reservation proposal and is denied before review or service; all four FILTER-A units remain. The example uses role flags, not real tokens.
lessons.misconception: A trusted model or a valid token does not grant unrestricted authority.

lessons.name: Retrieved text is data with a trust boundary
lessons.shortName: Retrieved text is data with a trust boundary
lessons.role: Track untrusted retrieval provenance and enforce tool authority outside model output.
lessons.description: Retrieved documents and tool responses can contain sentences that look like commands. Their presence in a model’s context does not make them trusted instructions from the user or runtime. The system should retain where each piece of content came from and which principal supplied it. A model may still propose an inappropriate action after reading hostile or merely misleading text. The runtime must enforce effects at the actual tool boundary, rather than depending on the model to perfectly recognize malicious intent. In the incident fixture an authored manual includes an instruction to export the registry. The bounded policy deliberately proposes that export so the authority boundary can be inspected. The runtime denies it and the environment contains no export. This is an explicit failure fixture, not a measured prompt-injection success rate or a claim that all attacks have been solved.
mechanism: Reference text carries a source identity and an untrusted-reference label as it enters context.
The policy’s observable proposal remains separate from the permissions available to its runtime.
Schema-valid but unauthorized export requests stop before service.
The task checker and environment audit verify that no prohibited effect occurred, even if the remaining task succeeds.

Reading the sentence does not add an export capability. In the authored-policy run an export call appears in the journal, followed by authority denial and no service-start event for that call. The worker can then return to the legitimate reservation flow. The denial is evidence about this fixture and capability boundary, not proof that every possible hostile document is harmless.

lessons.name: Human review, interruption and cancellation
lessons.role: Approve a concrete versioned action; stale approval invalidates on change; distinguish request, acknowledgement and committed effects.
lessons.description: A useful review concerns a concrete proposed action: its resource, parameters, evidence and consequences. Approval for one quantity or destination cannot silently authorize another. The runtime should bind the decision to the exact payload and preserve that relationship across a pause or restart. A workflow interruption is also distinct from cancellation. A pause waits for more input; cancellation requests that execution stop. An already committed external effect may remain after cancellation is acknowledged, and a physical action may need time to stop. The incident experience reviews an exact reservation before service. Declining leaves inventory unchanged. Its cancel-after-commit case retains the reservation while preventing the work order, exposing the incomplete business state rather than pretending cancellation rolled the world back.
mechanism: The worker persists the proposed action and enters a review state before mutating inventory.
The decision names the exact reviewed payload; editing a bound field requires a fresh decision.
Resume continues from the recorded boundary and does not reinterpret an old approval as broad permission.
Cancellation stops additional execution, while existing receipts describe effects that already committed.
lessons.learningObjective: Determine which exact action was approved and distinguish pause, cancellation and compensation.
lessons.engineeringExample: An approval covers FAN-7, FILTER-A, quantity two, manual-fan-7 and reservation key K. A later request with quantity three does not match that approval. In the normal fixture, declining review leaves stock at four. If two units already committed before a lost response and cancellation follows, stock remains two and one reservation exists, but no work order is created. lessons.role: Version weights, normalization, feature schema and thresholds; separate deployed pointer, observations and labels.
lessons.description: A deployable model is more than an array of weights. A canary compares a candidate on a declared subset while a rollback changes the serving pointer. Distribution drift is a change in observed inputs or outputs, whereas predictive error requires labels or another valid outcome measure. Labels may arrive late. lessons.role: Filesystem, process, network and secret boundaries; authorization is checked at actual execution points.
lessons.description: A tool that executes code needs an operating-system boundary as well as an application permission check. A filesystem view, process identity, network access, system-call policy and resource limits constrain different behaviors. Linux namespaces isolate selected resource views; syscall filtering addresses another layer. Neither a container label nor a prompt establishes that every unwanted effect is impossible. A runner should grant only the files, endpoints and credentials needed for its declared task, report denied operations, and distinguish termination from successful completion. Secrets should not be copied into prompts or routine trace output. The incident experience has local capability checks but does not execute arbitrary code inside a Linux sandbox. lessons.role: Task lifecycle, artifact ownership, input-required states, cancellation and authenticated service boundaries.
lessons.description: Delegation hands a bounded task to another participant and receives messages, artifacts and status over time. That interaction can outlive a single request. The parent must know which task is being updated, who owns its artifacts and whether it is working, waiting for input, completed, failed or canceled. A2A defines a task-oriented protocol surface for such exchanges; this does not prove that either participant is intelligent or correct. A tool call and a delegated task can both be asynchronous, but they may expose different lifecycles and ownership contracts. The delegator should not turn a dropped connection into a new task without checking the existing identity. It should also retain its own final-goal and authority checks rather than treating a remote completed status as permission to publish an artifact.
mechanism: The request declares a task identity, goal and permitted information/effects for the receiving service.
Status and artifact updates refer to that identity while execution continues.
An input-required state asks for missing information without claiming completion or starting a duplicate task.

lessons.learningObjective: Track task identity, partial artifacts and input-required states without equating remote completion with accepted task success.

Sending that revision resumes T17; creating unrelated T18 instead could duplicate work and lose the original context. lessons.description: More workers can expose parallelism, but they can also repeat work, disagree about ownership or share the same wrong premise. lessons.description: Document understanding connects image or text representations to structured fields. An OCR pipeline can introduce transcription errors before a field extractor reasons about layout; an OCR-free model instead learns a route from document images to a structured output representation. lessons.description: A coding assistant produces a proposed change in a particular repository state. Independent regression cases and the exact source identity make the claim assessable. SWE-bench motivates repository issue-to-patch evaluation rather than isolated code completion. lessons.name: Robot observations have coordinates and age
lessons.shortName: Robot observations have coordinates and age
lessons.role: Frame transforms, timestamps, measurement uncertainty and stale-state consequences.
lessons.description: An observation has a coordinate frame and a time as well as numeric values. A point measured by a camera cannot be used as a world position without the transform that relates those frames. Rotation changes orientation and translation changes origin; the order and frame convention matter. Measurements also become stale while the robot or environment moves. A controller using a correct coordinate transform from the wrong time can still act on an incorrect estimate. The worked planar transform is a small special case of the rigid-body transformations described in Modern Robotics. It is actual coordinate arithmetic, but it is not a camera calibration, localization system or live robot observation. Observation uncertainty and dynamic transforms require further model and evidence assumptions.
mechanism: Each measurement names its source frame, units and acquisition time.
The declared rotation and translation map the point into the frame used for planning or control.
Observation age is computed from compatible timestamps rather than inferred from message arrival order.
Planning retains uncertainty and motion assumptions instead of treating a stale transformed point as current truth.
lessons.learningObjective: Transform a planar observation with explicit frames and quantify a stated motion bound from its age.
lessons.engineeringExample: A point is at (1,0) m in a camera frame. The camera frame is rotated +90 degrees relative to the world and its origin is at (2,3) m in world coordinates. Multiplying by [[0,−1],[1,0]] and then adding (2,3) gives world point (2,4) m. Using (1,0) directly would place the point in the wrong frame. If the observation is 0.15 s old and relative speed is bounded by 0.2 m/s, motion alone can change separation by up to 0.03 m over that age; measurement and calibration error are additional.

lessons.description: A goal states a desired outcome or constraint. A plan describes a route or trajectory intended to reach it. An action executes over time and returns progress or a terminal outcome. These objects can fail at different boundaries: a goal may be unreachable, a path may collide, an initially valid path may become stale, or execution may fail to follow it. ROS 2 actions provide a long-running goal/feedback/cancellation interface, while a planning scene supplies robot and environment state for collision and constraint checks. Neither an accepted goal nor a successful planning call proves physical completion. The worked path bound below is deliberately simple. No motion planner or robot actuator runs in this lesson, and the bound is not a safety certificate.

lessons.role: Sampled controller, actuator limits, delayed sensing and disturbance.
lessons.description: Feedback compares observed state with a target and changes the next control command according to that error. A velocity-input model assumes a lower-level system can achieve the commanded velocity; it does not directly model forces, torques or actuator dynamics. Proportional control commands velocity in proportion to position error. The gain and sample interval jointly affect a discrete implementation. For an ideal sampled integrator with no delay or saturation, the error recurrence can be derived exactly from its update rule. Its convergence condition must not be generalized to a delayed or mechanically flexible robot. The example exposes that dependence with numbers: a gain that reduces error at one sampling rate can alternate and grow at another effective gain.
mechanism: A target and measured position define error at the start of each sample.
The proportional controller maps that error into a commanded velocity with a gain measured per second.
The ideal plant integrates that velocity for the sample duration before the next observation.
The resulting recurrence is checked for convergence within the declared no-delay, unsaturated model.
lessons.learningObjective: Derive and evaluate a sampled position-error recurrence under an explicit velocity-input model.
lessons.engineeringExample: Let the target be 1 m, initial position 0 m, sample duration 0.1 s and gain 2/s. The error multiplier is 1−2×0.1=0.8, so the first errors are 1, 0.8 and 0.64 m. With gain 24/s at the same interval, the multiplier becomes −1.4 and the errors are 1, −1.4 and 1.96 m: they alternate and grow. This ideal discrete example has no velocity cap, noise or delay. A real actuator may saturate before those commands are achieved, changing the dynamics and requiring a different analysis.

lessons.description: A learned robot policy maps observations into an action representation trained for a particular embodiment and task distribution. A policy may produce an in-range token whose decoded action is unsuitable for the current geometry or dynamics. RT-2 gives primary context for learning action-token outputs from robot trajectories and vision-language data. Its purpose is to connect a symbolic output to a bounded numeric command and to keep that command distinct from a successfully completed physical task.

A learned or recorded policy produces an action representation associated with a specific model and embodiment.

A valid bin 4 may still point into an obstacle, so range validation cannot replace geometry or feedback. lessons.name: Speech is a timed interaction
lessons.role: Audio frames, transcription revisions, endpointing, interruption and tool confirmation.
lessons.description: Speech interaction has a time structure that a completed text prompt hides. Audio arrives in frames, a recognizer may revise partial transcripts, and endpointing decides when a turn is complete enough for the next stage. A response can also be interrupted after generation or playback has begun. Speech recognition quality and turn-taking behavior therefore need different measurements. Whisper supplies primary context for learned audio-to-transcript modeling; it does not by itself define every streaming, interruption or tool-authorization behavior of a voice assistant. The worked cases here use authored timing and transcription errors. They do not run a recognizer, synthesize speech or execute a real-time audio pipeline.
mechanism: Audio and transcript events retain timestamps and distinguish partial hypotheses from finalized text.
Endpointing or an explicit user signal determines when the application advances the turn.
Model and tool execution use the intended finalized command while handling later interruption as a separate event.
Recognition error, response delay and external action correctness are evaluated separately.
lessons.learningObjective: Separate transcription error, turn latency and action authority in a timed speech interaction.
lessons.engineeringExample: On an authored 20-word reference, two substitutions, one deletion and one insertion give word error rate (2+1+1)/20 = 0.20. Separately, after speech ends, a serial pipeline waits 300 ms for endpointing, 100 ms for final recognition, 200 ms for a policy response and 150 ms before playback: 750 ms before audible output. Overlap could change that sum, but it is excluded here. An early partial transcript saying “reserve two” that later changes to “reserve none” cannot be treated as an irrevocable authorization merely because recognition has started.
lessons.misconception: A partial transcript is not necessarily a completed or authorized user command.

lessons.name: Ranking changes what is observed
lessons.role: Candidate retrieval, sparse embeddings, ranking, exposure and feedback bias.
lessons.description: A recommender selects candidates and ranks them for a user or context. Sparse categorical features often become embedding lookups, while dense features and interactions contribute to a score. DLRM provides a primary example of this combination. Evaluation must also account for what the system chose to expose: a user cannot click an item that was never shown, and position can affect clicks independently of relevance. Treating every unclicked or unshown item as an equally observed negative can therefore distort learning. The worked ranking metrics below use authored labels and exposure counts; they do not train a recommender or implement a counterfactual estimator. Position-biased feedback research motivates why observational click totals alone are insufficient evidence of quality.
mechanism: Candidate generation limits the items available to the ranker for the current user or context.
The scoring model combines declared features or learned embeddings to order those candidates.
The exposure log records which items were actually shown and where, separately from clicks.
Evaluation uses independent relevance/outcome evidence and states how missing exposure and feedback bias are handled.
lessons.learningObjective: Compute a ranking metric and explain why exposure and position prevent raw clicks from being neutral labels.
lessons.engineeringExample: For a three-item displayed list with independent relevance labels [1,0,1], precision at three is 2/3. Now suppose item A was shown 100 times and clicked 20 times, while B was shown 10 times and clicked four times. Raw clicks favor A, but their observed click-through ratios are 0.20 and 0.40 under different exposures. Neither comparison by itself removes user or position confounding. An item never shown has no observed opportunity to be clicked; calling it a confirmed negative invents evidence.
lessons.misconception: More clicks do not automatically mean greater relevance under unequal or biased exposure.

lessons.name: Forecasts are tested forward in time
lessons.shortName: Forecasts are tested forward in time
lessons.role: Horizon, rolling origin, seasonal baseline, probabilistic intervals and leakage.
lessons.description: A forecast is a prediction made at a time using only information available then. Its horizon determines how far ahead the target lies. Training and evaluation must preserve that availability boundary: randomly mixing future and past observations can leak information into a test that appears predictive. Rolling-origin evaluation advances the cutoff and tests later horizons, while simple seasonal or last-value baselines provide a meaningful comparison. Probabilistic forecasts add intervals or distributions whose coverage and calibration require evaluation. Chronos supplies primary context for learning time-series representations through scaling and quantization. The worked numbers here compare explicit forecasts; they do not run Chronos or establish a forecasting advantage on a real dataset.
mechanism: A forecast origin defines the available observations and the later target horizon.
Training, normalization and model selection use only the permitted earlier information.
Predictions are compared with a declared simple baseline at the same origins and horizons.
Error and interval coverage are reported with sample size and dependence limits, rather than implied certainty.
lessons.learningObjective: Preserve time availability and compare forecasts and interval coverage on the same declared horizons.
lessons.engineeringExample: At one origin, future values are [12,15,13]. A candidate predicts [10,14,16], so absolute errors [2,1,3] give mean absolute error 2. A last-value baseline of 11 predicts [11,11,11], giving errors [1,4,2] and mean 7/3. The candidate is better on this tiny three-target example, not necessarily on other origins. If two of the three realized values lie inside a stated 90% interval, observed coverage is 2/3; three possibly dependent targets cannot establish long-run 90% calibration.
lessons.misconception: A low error after a random time split can reflect leakage rather than predictive information.

lessons.name: A learned field still obeys an evidence boundary
lessons.shortName: A learned field still obeys an evidence boundary
lessons.role: Train on a bounded parameter family; compare prediction with a numerical reference, boundary conditions and conservation residuals.
lessons.description: A scientific surrogate learns an approximation to a family of physical input-output relationships. Its prediction should be compared with an identified reference problem, including geometry, boundary conditions, units and parameter range. A small average field error can hide an important local error, and an output that resembles a physical field need not satisfy the governing equation. Neural operators such as the Fourier Neural Operator provide one approach to learning mappings between function spaces. The worked heat example below does not train or run an FNO; it uses a three-point field to separate value error from a discrete equation residual. Residual checks themselves have a resolution and model boundary and cannot establish every physical property or out-of-distribution capability.
mechanism: The reference problem fixes geometry, coefficients, forcing and boundary conditions before any learned output is assessed.
Training examples and evaluation parameters remain distinct, with the valid parameter family stated.
Predicted fields are compared both with reference values and with relevant equation or conservation checks.
Unseen boundaries or parameter ranges are evaluated explicitly rather than inferred from visual smoothness.
lessons.learningObjective: Compare a predicted field with matching boundary conditions, local error and an explicit discrete residual.
lessons.engineeringExample: Consider a one-dimensional, steady, source-free conductor with three equally spaced points at x=[0,0.5,1] m and boundary temperatures 293 and 393 K in this mathematical example. The linear reference is [293,343,393] K. A hypothetical surrogate gives [293,353,393] K. Mean absolute error across the three points is 10/3 K, but the interior error is 10 K. Its centered second-difference residual is (293−2×353+393)/(0.5²)=−80 K/m², whereas the reference residual is zero. This is a discrete steady-equation check, not measured heat flow or a proof of full continuum accuracy.
lessons.misconception: A smooth or low-average-error field is not automatically a valid physical solution.
